extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, and students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing prosecution of patent applications before the Patent Office (communications, motions, appeals) and the law of abandonment (what constitutes abandonment of an application or of the invention, statutory two‑year rule, excuses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal limited to issues on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: “The appeal is limited to the issues apparent on the record, and brings up only the particular adjudications of which complaint is made. An appeal raising no issue will be summarily dismissed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals cannot be used to raise new matters not apparent on the record; appellate review is confined to the specific adjudications complained of. (Cases cited: Ex parte Evarts, Ex parte Jones, Jenkins v. Barney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of new evidence on appeal requires remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence is admitted during an appeal to support the claims of the applicant against references and objections of the examiner, or to vary the issues of fact concerning patentability of the invention, the whole case must be remanded to the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appellate forum will not decide newly-formed factual issues; introduction of evidence that changes factual issues requires remand so the examiner can reconsider in light of that evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner acts in judicial appellate capacity; finality limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In an appeal from the examiners-in-chief to the Commissioner, he acts only in a judicial capacity and as a court of appellate jurisdiction; cases decided by him on appeal will not be re-opened except by himself, and predecessors' decisions will not be reviewed except in accordance with rules governing new trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner’s appellate decisions have strong finality within the Office; examiners-in-chief cannot rehear cases after they cease to be pending without written authority from the Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications with examiners should be in writing; interview timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules generally direct that communications between the Office and applicants or their attorneys should take place in writing. Interviews with examiners concerning applications may be had at the examiner's rooms during office hours or at times specially authorized by the Commissioner, but no personal discussion of a pending application is allowed until after the first official action thereon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants/attorneys should prefer written communications; personal interviews are tightly controlled and generally only after the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions must be made and determined by tribunal where case is pending
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions proper to be made at all must be made and determined by the tribunal before which the case is pending at the time; cases are regarded as pending before a given tribunal until an appeal is taken or the time for appeal has expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to shift or re-raise motions in a different tribunal while the case remains pending; procedural posture controls where motions are heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path of appeal depends on nature of motion (form vs substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an adverse decision on a motion must be taken to the Commissioner if the motion involves only matters of form, but to the examiners-in-chief if it relates to matters of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify motions as procedural/formal or substantive to determine proper appellate route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion once decided without appeal cannot be renewed on same facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion once made and determined without appeal cannot be renewed on the same facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties cannot relitigate a motion that was decided and not appealed unless there are new facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct governed by rules in force at inception
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of each case is governed by the rules in force at its inception, unless new rules are adopted which can be followed without prejudice to the applicant, in which event the latter rules prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural changes generally do not retroactively alter the tribunal's obligations unless they can be applied without harming the applicant; tribunal reorganizations do not interrupt pending applications though modes of procedure may change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: abandonment of application vs abandonment of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandonment of the application is not an abandonment of the invention. Abandonment of the invention causes loss of all right to apply and obtain a patent; abandonment of the application places the inventor as if he never filed one, and a later application may be subject to objections arising in the intervening time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning an application exposes the inventor to intervening public uses, sales, or advances in the art that could defeat a later application; legal effect and remedies differ between the two kinds of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of abandoning an application: intervening public use/sale and advances in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: By abandoning the application the date of the applicant's application is transferred to the day of the new application; publications, patents, inventions, or intermediate public use/sale occurring after abandonment may be cited against a later application and may defeat claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning an application risks that subject-matter which would have been safe under the original filing date becomes unpatentable because of intervening disclosures or uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory two‑year completion/prosecution rule (prima facie abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law provides that all applications must be completed and prepared for examination within two years after filing the petition, and failure thereof should be considered abandoned unless the Commissioner is satisfied the delay was unavoidable; additionally failure to prosecute within two years after any action of which notice has been given shall also work abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two years is the statutory benchmark triggering a prima facie presumption of abandonment; the applicant bears the burden to justify delay to the Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two years is prima facie; unreasonable delay can be shorter or longer
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's two‑year rule does not confer an absolute right to two years of inaction between each Office action; unreasonable delay for any period is abandonment, and the two‑year period is only prima facie unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even delays shorter than two years can be deemed unreasonable in some circumstances; conversely, delays longer than two years may be excused if unavoidable and satisfactorily shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Last action" defined for computing delay
rubrics_metrics.description: "Last action" is the last interlocutory action of the Patent Office affecting the progress of the application, followed by the mailing of a notice of such action to the applicant. Ministerial acts (e.g., returning a model, sending a routine letter) do not constitute "last action." A suspension of action implies further action and is not the "last action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute statutory delay from the last substantive interlocutory Office action (excluding purely ministerial acts); suspensions do not stop the clock as a 'last action'.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Inaction" of applicant defined
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant's 'inaction' is his failure to perform the act devolving upon him in order to advance his case. Letters of general inquiry, unimportant amendments, or other trivial acts do not prevent the two‑year period from running; the applicant must take action that obliges the Office to act in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid abandonment, applicants must take substantive steps that propel prosecution; perfunctory communications will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Day of "last action" excluded when computing two years
rubrics_metrics.description: In computing the two‑year period of inactivity the day on which the 'last action' of the Patent Office was performed is excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the exclusion rule when calculating statutory time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable delay excuse standard; Commissioner as primary adjudicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The inaction of the applicant cannot prejudice his application if the delay was unavoidable. The Commissioner is the final judge within the Office on whether delay was unavoidable, though courts may adjudicate abandonment-of-invention issues. 'Unavoidable delay' must be clearly proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted excuses include poverty, protracted sickness, inevitable absence from the country, or legal inability to pursue rights — but the applicant must demonstrate the unavoidable nature of the delay, typically for the entire statutory period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable delay must cover entire period and be proven; leniency limited
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unavoidable' delay in prosecuting an application means unavoidable during the entire two years; delay unaccompanied by effort to avoid it is not 'unavoidable.' Too great leniency to delaying applicants, to the prejudice of the public, must not be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial or intermittent excuses are weak; courts/Commissioner require clear proof that all periods of inactivity were unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delays caused by others or Office errors may excuse applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where inaction is ultimately due to errors or misconduct of other persons, without the applicant's knowledge or beyond his control, delays in the Patent Office not attributable to him, mistakes in the Office, or neglect of his attorney (if not acquiesced in) may be accepted as excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that delay was outside applicant's control and not acquiesced in; Office mistakes or reliable agent failure can sometimes preserve the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay motivated by personal interest or indifference not excused
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant has been led to delay by motives of personal interest, or even by mere indifference to the rights of others, he must be held strictly to the statutory penalties and cannot be relieved; pecuniary interest or engagement in other occupations is not an excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not excuse self-interested or indifferent inaction; show bona fide inability to act rather than choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by express written declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be abandoned by the express act of the applicant; such abandonment must be in writing, describing the application by the title of the invention and the date of filing, signed by the applicant in person, and filed in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal written abandonment must meet these description/signature/filing requirements; do not rely on informal statements to effect abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a new application does not automatically withdraw the earlier one
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation of a new application for the same invention does not withdraw or abandon the original; each is accepted and treated by the Office as independent unless the later is offered as an amendment to or substitute for the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing later applications without explicit withdrawal may leave the earlier application intact unless an express abandonment occurs; relation between filings depends on abandonment status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and substitution: before/after final rejection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time before final rejection or allowance an application may be withdrawn and a new application filed with new specification, oath, drawings, and a new fee. After final rejection a new one may also be filed, though the rejected application cannot be withdrawn. The relation of the new to the old depends on whether the original was abandoned; an abandoned application can never be revived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend to maintain priority or benefit from the earlier filing date, beware that abandonment severs that benefit; procedural formalities and fees required for substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation of all claims constitutes abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation of all the claims is abandonment of the application; a power of attorney that gives full authority to amend does not authorize withdrawal of all claims so as to destroy the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broad cancellations without understanding abandonment consequences; ensure agent authority is carefully limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long lapse after withdrawal treated as abandonment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: On a question of abandonment of the invention by withdrawal of the application, the lapse of time is of great weight, if not conclusive (e.g., delays of many years after withdrawal have been held to constitute abandonment of the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial post-withdrawal inaction will be evidence (often conclusive) that the inventor abandoned the invention to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension at applicant's request is inaction and may cause abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspension of an application at the request of the applicant, and at his option to proceed with it, is 'inaction,' and unless taken up within two years it is abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary suspensions are risky — treat them as potential starts to the statutory clock.
